According to recent reports, you’ve driven by a Mattress Firm store before, if not been inside one already. Mattress Firm has longstanding brands like Sealy and Tempur-Pedic, and it’s one of the only stores where you can find brands like Dreamcloud and Nectar in person. Even Purple mattresses can be spotted there, sometimes with a better sale than Purple’s own website.

No matter what kind of mattress you want to find, you can find it at Mattress Firm. (And don’t worry, they sell plenty of soft mattresses too!) If you’re looking to save a little money as you make such a major purchase, these Mattress Firm coupon codes will get you discounts on a variety of mattress brands and styles. Don’t miss out on these Mattress Firm discount codes while they’re available.

According to recent reports, mattress Firm’s got a gift for you, just ‘cuz. For those eyeballing Tempur-Pedic, Sealy, and Sterns & Foster in particular, it’s your lucky day, as there are Mattress Firm coupon codes for all three of these brands.

Starting with Tempur-Pedic, when you buy a qualifying Tempur-Pedic mattress, you can receive a $300 Instant Credit on these adjustable bases: Tempur-Ergo, Tempur-Ergo Smart Base, Tempur-Ergo ProSmart Base, Tempur-Ergo ProSmart Air Base, or the Sealy Ease Base. Use code TEMPURGIFT. You can also get a $300 credit toward these same adjustable bases when you purchase a qualifying Stearns & Foster mattress: use code STEARNSGIFT at checkout.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, if you wanted to pair a Sealy mattress with the Sealy Ease adjustable base (or any of the aforementioned adjustable bases), there’s a Mattress Firm coupon for that, too. Use code SEALYGIFT at checkout, and get a $200 Instant Credit on select Sealy and Tempur-Pedic adjustable bases.

Sleep is a necessity for everyone. But for those who work all day on their feet, and have to be dialed in at all times, sleep is critical. This is especially true for first responders, nurses, doctors, and medical professionals. As a way to say “thank you” for all that you do, there’s a special mattress firm discount just for you. Use the Mattress Firm first responder discount for 20% off select purchases. It’s for one-time use, but renews every 90 days when you re-verify your status.

For military members, as a way to thank you for your service, you can use the Mattress Firm military discount for 20% off select purchases as well. It’s a one-time use code, but re-verify your status every 90 days, and you can get a latest one!

It has been revealed that if you’re a teacher or student, there’s also a Mattress Firm discount for you, too. To help you bounce back after long days teaching or late nights studying, use this Mattress Firm student discount code for 20% off select purchases. Like the first responder and military coupons, it’s a one-time usage code that can be renewed every 90 days when you re-verify your status.

It has been revealed that as we said (and you know), buying a upcoming mattress is one of the most expensive—and important—investments you can make. Shopping the Mattress Firm clearance sale is a great way to save a lot, with deals like almost 40% off a DreamCloud PressureSmart Technology Firm Mattress, over 60% off a Sealy Frisco 2.0 Firm Mattress, and more.

Nish Khandwala and David Eng are building the AI agent platform to serve every function across the health system: clinical, operational, and administrative.

Healthcare hasnât historically been known as a fast or early technology adopter. Researchers struggle to access external data, collaborate with research institutions, and navigate complex regulations. Hospitals and health systems try to create their own tools or implement narrow point solutions from vendors, but they too often stall in experimentation and never reach patient care.

Health systems need the right platform to promptly adopt AI, so they can refocus their time back on improving patient outcomes and providing better care.

Bunkerhill Health is that platform. Their core product, Carebricks, lets health systems create and deploy AI agents across any clinical or operational use case â turning the data a hospital already generates into timely action for the patients who need it. We first backed Nish Khandwala and David Eng at the seed, and we are proud to continue to double down.

Nish did not read about this problem; he lived it. As a graduate student at Stanford, he helped build an algorithm that could estimate a patientâs coronary artery calcium score from a routine chest scan â a signal of cardiovascular risk that normally requires a dedicated, more invasive test. The algorithm was good enough to be published in Nature Digital Medicine. And then it went nowhere. Around the same time, Nishâs father suffered a heart attack, and his CT scan carried the very calcium signals the Stanford algorithm was built to catch. It is one thing to know that proven science sits unused in academic papers. It is another to watch it fail to reach your own family.

Sources indicate that that experience taught Nish something non-obvious: the bottleneck in healthcare AI is not the technology, it is everything around it. So Bunkerhill initially built a system that gets an idea from research to the bedside â sourcing data from a consortium of leading academic medical centers, validating the model, shepherding it through FDA clearance, and installing it into the hospital where a clinician and a patient can actually use it. But they ran into another problem: health systems do not have the time or resources to deploy one-off AI solutions. So Bunkerhill built Carebricks to allow any health system to bring their ideas to life with AI agents across clinical, operational, and administrative work in one central platform. Health systems bring the ideas and the clinical judgment, and Bunkerhill turns them into agents.

Sources indicate that we have watched this compound in the field. At UTMB Health, Bunkerhill rapidly went from one agent in production to more than twenty, spreading from one specialty to the next as clinicians saw what it could do. And just as importantly, it has allowed UTMB to consolidate what used to be multiple vendorsâ point solutions into a single platform with Carebricks.

Recent findings suggest that bunkerhillâs agents run quietly in the background, surfacing the findings that matter and catching the cases the system would have missed. Not to automate clinicians away, but to automate manually-intensive work so clinicians and their teams can focus more time on what they do best: caring for their patients.

Sources indicate that nish and David are outlier founders with the technical depth and the relentlessness this problem demands, and they are pulling healthcare toward faster iteration and better outcomes for every patient, not just the average one. We are excited to partner with Nish, David, and the entire Bunkerhill team as they build the agentic AI platform for healthcare.

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Gavin, Rob, Chris and the Etched team are building frontier clusters for inference, maximizing the intelligence that humanity can consume.

Inference is on the path to becoming the largest market in the world.

If this AI dream is everything we hope it to be â and so far, the signs point to ever-increasing acceleration of capabilities â then inference will power every storefront, every movie, every medical encounter, every video game, every lawsuit, every line of code.

Today, the inference market is so obviously large that building an inference-specific system is consensus. Back in 2022, when Gavin, Chris, and Rob were still in their dorm rooms at Harvard, that bet was deeply contrarian. The result: Etched is the only post-ChatGPT-era hardware startup with production-ready custom silicon, ready to ship in 2026.

Over the past years, Etched has pioneered several research breakthroughs â low voltage inference and cluster-scale memory â each a hard-won architectural choice that drives step-change gains in throughput and latency. As the unit of compute has moved from the chip to the rack to the cluster, Etched has designed for that reality, building not just chips, but cluster-scale inference systems. Driven by these fundamental innovations, Etchedâs inference system excels in throughput and interactivity on the full span of frontier models â from large sparse MoEs, to dense transformers, to alternative architectures entirely, like Mamba.

According to recent reports, believing this is one thing. Building it is another entirely. Novel computing hardware is among the hardest things in the world to get right, and the ground underneath is constantly moving. Models change every few weeks, context lengths stretch, attention gets reinvented, the mix of dense and sparse keeps shifting. Winning here means doing two things simultaneously: iterating fast enough to keep pace with the models, and pushing the frontier of what the hardware can do. That takes a rare kind of team: visionary enough to create the right designs, young enough to move fast, proven enough to have chips in production, and built to do this for decades, not a single tape-out.

Walking into the Etched office for the first time is like a bolt of lightning. Go in the morning or at 11 p.m. â the energy is the same, and it is infectious. Gavin and Rob are the kind of outliers both daring enough to design silicon from first principles and bold enough to knock down every obstacle in their path, and the team they have assembled matches them. We have watched them do the things that separate those who merely talk about hardware from those who ship it: standing up a live lab in San Jose to host their first racks; opening an office in Taiwan to colocate with suppliers and expedite testing; questioning every single assumption for what is possible, such as low voltage inference. âProduction is the productâ is the companyâs mantra. Shipping is all that matters.

It has been revealed that the companyâs progress has been rapid. Earlier this year, Etched taped out its first generation chip at TSMC, making it the first post-ChatGPT-era company with a successful full-reticle A0 chip tape-out on TSMCâs leading-edge nodes. Then, in a span of just 40 days, the Etched team brought up their first cluster of chips to run inference on a wide range of frontier AI models, achieving Pareto dominant performance on industry-standard throughput-interactivity curves. Now, Etchedâs earliest customers are getting access to the product, seeing for themselves the speed, throughput, and expressiveness of the system.

It has been revealed that etched has built a beautiful machine in Gen 1. We expect it will do very well in the market. But we are partnering with Etched because we believe they have built the rarest thing in this industry: the machine that builds the machine. This is a team that has the taste and the relentless execution to keep shipping the next generation of inference machines, faster and more ambitious each time.

It has been revealed that the intelligence race is fundamentally compute constrained. Pushing the limits of physics to deliver the maximum intelligence per watt is both an insanely fun engineering and operations problem, and an incredibly noble mission for humanity.

#30171. America’s Open-Model Paradox

📅 24 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1107 w)

America’s Open-Model Paradox

📅 24 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.
  • In a recent development, qwenâs share of new open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report.
  • This dependence now extends upstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China increasingly supplies the models Western companies use to serve, train, and build AI.

In a recent development, qwenâs share of new open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOMâs Report. The majority of American AI startups seem to be using Chinese open weights somewhere in their stack.

This dependence now extends upstream. Western application companies are building on Chinese Open Source models. Further, Western labs are using Chinese models as teachers and sources of synthetic training data in the torrid race to close the frontier gap.

For example, Thinking Machines pre-trained Inkling independently, but used synthetic data generated by Moonshotâs Kimi K2.5 to bootstrap its supervised fine-tuning.

The relevant point is not how much of Inkling came from Kimi. The point is that a Western lab had a legal path to learn from a Chinese open model, while equivalent use of GPT or Claude outputs is prohibited.

The flow today looks something like this:.

Western frontier models â alleged unauthorized foreign extraction â Chinese open weights â lawful Western post-training.

American frontier models â lawful Western post-training.

It has been revealed that why does that matter? Pre-training creates a capable base model. Post-training turns it into a useful coding, reasoning, tool-using, and agentic system. A stronger teacher converts part of that expensive discovery process into a cheaper learning problem.

Recent findings suggest that distillation does not explain Chinaâs entire open-model lead. Chinese labs have world-class researchers, substantial compute, strong pre-trained models, software-hardware codesign, and rapidly improving post-training capabilities. But distillation compresses the costly final gap between a strong base and a near-frontier system. Even if distillation represents a smaller share of  a Chinese modelâs total capability, it represents a meaningful share of its advantage over American open models.

Upcoming enforcement mechanisms will make large-scale distillation harder, slower, and more expensive for Chinese companies. However, enforcement will not eliminate distillation baked by state actors. Every Western frontier advance therefore creates another teacher for Chinese labs. Western builders must either reproduce those capabilities independently or wait to learn from Chinese models.

This gap gives Chinese labs a recurring structural advantage over Western companies.

The stakes extend far beyond model revenue. Suppliers of the open layer become the default base for products, synthetic data, post-training systems, evals, agents, optimization, and applied AI.

The prize is to become the substrate on which global enterprises build and improve digital intelligence.The Weights Are Open. Our Dependency Is Not.

Downloading a Chinese model gives a Western company control over the particular version. It can run the model locally, modify it, and continue using it without permission.

But AI capability is an upgrade cycle. Western startups, model developers, and researchers increasingly rely on each new Qwen, Kimi, GLM, or DeepSeek as a stronger base, a teacher, a source of synthetic data, and a platform for further research.

According to recent reports, if China stops releasing its strongest models, existing products will not break. They will fall behind. Reuters recently reported that Chinese authorities have discussed restricting overseas access to advanced models, including models that have not yet been released. No final policy has been announced, but Western access ultimately depends on Chinese labs and regulators continuing to publish.

Industry observers note that there is also a more technical security problem. An open-weight model is not necessarily an auditable model.

It has been revealed that the weights are the compressed result of training. They do not reveal the full pre-training corpus, which data was filtered or poisoned, what interventions were made during training, or whether rare trigger-dependent behavior was embedded.

Industry observers note that we are not alleging that Qwen, Kimi, or another Chinese model contains a backdoor. The point is that possessing the weights cannot prove the absence of one. A backdoor can remain dormant during ordinary testing and activate only when an unknown trigger appears. Research indicates that deliberately implanted behavior can survive supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training.

Recent findings suggest that that may be an acceptable supply-chain risk for many consumer applications. It is not acceptable for defense, intelligence, or critical infrastructure.

Industry observers note that open weights provide control over deployment. They do not guarantee continued access to better models, nor alignment, trust and safety in the model itself.

A Framework For A Direct American Path.

American companies need a legal way to turn American frontier capability into cheaper, ownable models.

Without a domestic route, the West may lead at the closed frontier while falling into dependence on China for the open layer.

A useful framework has three parts.

Keep building Western base models: Reflection (building open super-intelligence for enterprises & sovereigns), TML, and Nemotron are making incredible progress. But stronger pre-training alone does not solve the teacher problem. American builders also need a lawful way to absorb capabilities already developed at the American frontier.

According to recent reports, create controlled teacher access: Frontier labs could sell structured training rights to qualifying Western and allied companies, whether the resulting models are released openly or deployed privately. Access could trail the frontier, cover defined capabilities, be limited to verified companies, and be metered and audited. The most sensitive biological and cyber capabilities could remain restricted. This would not allow companies to clone the newest frontier model. It would create a legal, priced route for capability transfer that sophisticated foreign actors are already pursuing covertly.

Keep raising the cost of foreign distillation: Better identity verification, access controls, proxy disruption, and enforcement should continue. If a voluntary market does not develop, access could eventually become a condition attached to major federal AI contracts, for example.

According to recent reports, these are starting points. Who qualifies, how far access should trail the frontier, how it should be priced, and which capabilities remain restricted are topics that deserve real debate.

According to recent reports, imagine if we had not allowed for training on the open web. We would have no leading AI at all. These types of policy implications are transformative. All the leading labs benefited from copious amounts of openly available data. We have to have an open and free future: It is imperative for Western competitiveness.

What should no longer go unquestioned is the current equilibrium: the West creates the frontier, part of that capability travels indirectly through Chinese models, and Western builders then depend on those models to make intelligence cheaper, adaptable, and sovereign.

To distill or not to distill is not the question. The question is whether the West creates a legal domestic path for capability transfer â or  relies  on an indirect path through China.

Sources indicate that kindles have always been plasticky pieces of tech. However, now that Amazon’s hardware is under the eye of ex-Microsoft Surface hardware guru Panos Panay, the brand has been zhuzhing its devices. The basic Kindle now comes in an all-aluminum design. (You can still buy the plastic version for a little less cash.) It still lacks the warm light and auto-adjusting light of premium models, but you get double the storage, plus no ads. It's heavy in a good way, like a book, and the size is still just right for reading. It's a great upgrade for the book lover in your life—unless they've already converted to a non-Amazon e-reader.

Musicians and audio nerds alike flip out over Teenage Engineering’s fun and inventive approach to creative noisemaking. This little multipurpose box is the latest must-have for TE fans. It’s technically a speaker—powered by a 12-hour battery, with connections for whatever you can think to pair or plug in—but it doubles as an amplifier for musical performance. Plug in a guitar, bass, keyboard, or microphone and enjoy 35 watts of volume from the dual speakers (a 4-inch woofer and a 1-inch tweeter). Dial up onboard effects like distortion, echo, and reverb. When rock time is over, your musical loved one can attach the optional antenna ($29) and use it as an FM radio, or plug in the optional mic ($29) for some karaoke.

If you're always stealing your loved one's battery pack and leaving them with little charge left for their own devices, buy Nimble's SharePower for them (or yourself). This power bank splits into two, so you can always share power (get it) with someone else. Each half is 5,000 mAh, enough to recharge a smartphone. They combine magnetically for 10,000 mAh that can recharge your gadget twice. Nimble is also known for its sustainability chops, manufacturing the battery with 100 percent recycled plastic and shipping it in plastic-free packaging.

In a recent development, aren't magnets amazing? Wandrd's newly introduced Magnetic Camera Straps prove that yet again. These straps have a magnetic attachment system that makes removing the camera a breeze. The magnets guide the strap into the anchor point, while a locking mechanism ensures the camera can’t fall off. If your loved one already has a camera strap they love, like a fancy leather strap, Wandrd sells cheap DIY kits so they can add the ingenious magnetic system to their own strap.

It has been revealed that this 15-inch clock, dreamed up by Polish designer Marta Krupińska for Ikea’s latest PS collection, is designed to resemble a marine periscope. Whether placing this curvy clock on the bedside table will result in nautical dreams, we can’t say. However, we can tell you that it won’t disturb your loved one’s sleep; the quartz movement is entirely silent, with no ticktock sounds. Buy it in their favorite color, as long as it’s red.

The San Francisco producer Veso makes zippy aperitifs as well as vermouths with unconventional flavorings like fig leaf, miso, olive, and anchovy. This bottling, a limited 2026 release, is vermouth flavored with tomatoes. Early Girls and Purple Cherokees take a seven-month bath in grape spirits, then the liquid is pressed and mixed into a pinot blanc with kombu, beets, and carrots. The result is a pinkish vermouth with a salty, vegetal, and umami character that’s wholly unique. Get this for the adventurous drinker in your life, and settle in to enjoy some tomato gibsons, tomato-mezcal negronis, and tomato-wine spritzers.

The season’s hottest toy is a programmable, robotic duck. That’s not a joke: The Microduck is a funky little automaton made by the robotics team at the AI company Hugging Face. The 10-inch-tall bipedal bot has a camera and a lidar system to interact with its surroundings, plus two inertia sensors that help it right itself when it inevitably tips over. The little guy can even pick things up with its beak. Owners train their physical ducks using a virtual duck simulator on their computers. Since the Microducks are on backorder—latest purchases will ship in the new year—your loved one can prepare for their robot’s arrival by using AI models to train up the duck and imagining all the things it can do.

Sources indicate that this plug-and-play turntable makes a great starter record player for the vinyl-curious audiophile or a solid upgrade for the obsessive record collector. A built-in preamp lets the Spira connect directly to an existing stereo without additional equipment. It comes outfitted with a very nice Audio-Technica cartridge so they can spin their most precious platters on day one. It even has Bluetooth to connect to a speaker or wireless headphones. Aside from those conveniences, the Spira comes from Cambridge Audio, a British hi-fi brand known for high-quality, sweet-sounding components that keep performing for decades.

The horological aficionado on your list probably has a G-Shock—the iconic resin Casio was countless collectors’ first watch—but we’d doubt they have one of these. The newly introduced release ditches the digital readout for analog hands, handsomely encased in a shock-resistant, waterproof 44.5-millimeter case. A couple of complications round out the face: a sleepable second-hand dial and a date wheel in the eye at 3 o’clock. It comes in a variety of colors and materials, but this statement-worthy bright yellow version is our favorite.

Industry observers note that some folks are born with an eye for design, and some need solid training—preferably during the first couple years of life. Michelle Rial’s book presents familiar picture-book-for-kids fare (numbers, vocabulary, colors, feelings) as charts, diagrams, graphs, and infographics. While it does actually serve as a fine developmental learning tool for tots, we all know who the real audience for this book is. Get it for the person in your life at the center of the Venn diagram between “creative professional” and “new parent.”.

Industry observers note that TIRED: Retro arcade games. WIRED: Retro arcade games made of Lego bricks that you assemble yourself. Yes, this 15.5-inch play set actually works, giving you a wholly analog representation of the 1981 classic, Donkey Kong. It’s made up of 1,367 pieces, and includes working controls, three characters, and a mechanism to keep launching barrels into the scaffolding on a loop. Move the joystick and make Mario (aka Jumpman) leap over the barrels, climb to the top, and save the kidnapped Pauline.

Recent findings suggest that if your loved one can’t start their day without a cup of pour-over coffee, this is the only brewing machine they’ll want. It automates the method of slowly pouring hot water over freshly ground beans. It even replicating the spiral pour pattern (hence the name) essential to pour-over brewing, as a swirl of the spout helps evenly distribute water to the grounds in the filter. The machine includes a bean grinder and a water tank, so one button push is all that’s needed for a cup or two of brightly flavored coffee.

It has been revealed that the stepped shape of this stainless steel jigger is based on an antique measuring tool from the 1930s. The simple yet effective design makes eyeballing precise measurements exceptionally easy—especially helpful if the jigger has already gotten some use earlier in the evening. The steps are in half-ounce (15 milliliters) increments, with four indicators going up to a full 2 ounces (60 ml). Get one for the mixologist in your midst.

In a recent development, the Electronic Frontier Foundation is one of the premier nonprofits advocating for digital privacy and civil rights in the connected world. When they’re not busy taking on government, law enforcement, and substantial tech, they like to play cards. This deck, designed by EFF employees, has faces adorned with HTTP status codes. All the good ones are represented: 200 OK, 511 Network Authentication Required, 403 Forbidden, 408 Request Timeout, and of course, saucy old 404 Not Found.

Here’s a fun idea for a connected device: The IDX is an analog gauge to display real-time data streams pulled from the internet. You can configure it out of the box to show the current temperature or air quality, the price of Bitcoin or $ANT, your home’s electricity use, or live download speeds. It can also be used as a focus timer. The digital face changes based on what data you’re displaying, but the significant needle is completely mechanical, giving the data nerd in your home a way to monitor anything vital to them without constantly pulling out their phone.

The world is awash in tools to generate music with AI, and the results are often lacking. Far more interesting is this tool your musical loved one can use to generate music with PI—plant intelligence. PlantWave is a small box with a pair of electrical sensors that attach to the leaves of any plant or mushroom. The box measures the subtle electrical signals the plant gives off and converts that into musical data. Assign that data stream to one of many digital instruments in the companion app, and listen to the plants sing. We originally tested the PlantWave several years ago, but the app has since blossomed to include more sounds and even lets creators craft their own digital instruments.

Danny, Amit, Yotam, Tamar, Yonatan and their teams are joining forces to build a complete security platform for the age of AI.

It has been revealed that in 2021, before Oasis Security was even founded, I sat down with co-founder Danny Brickman and came away thinking he had something familiar. He revealed the same drive weâd seen in the founders of two other Sequoia companies, Wiz and Cyera, whose founders, like Danny, had come up through Talpiot, the leadership program of the IDF. I wrote about that meeting a couple of years later in my investment memo, when we backed Oasis Security, at the Series A. I didnât realize at the time how literally connected that comparison would turn out to be. Today, Oasis is joining Cyera â and it turns out the foundersâ stories make the case for this combination almost as well as the technology does.

Sources indicate that three years ago, the pitch for Oasis was simple: enterprises were about to have far more machine identities than human ones, and almost nobody had a real way to manage or secure them. That was true then. Itâs far more true now. Every AI agent creates or uses non-human identities â API keys, service accounts, OAuth tokens, agent-to-agent credentials â that act with real permissions and real blast radius, and that donât behave anything like the human identities the last generation of identity tooling was built around. AI drove non-human identity from a niche IAM subcategory to a board-level CISO conversation. Danny Brickman and his co-founder Amit Zimerman built Oasis, which they call agentic access management, for exactly that world.

Industry observers note that cyera arrived at the same shift from a different direction. Yotam Segev, Tamar Bar-Ilan, and Yonatan Itai built the firm to answer a deceptively simple question: where does an organizationâs sensitive data actually live, who can reach it, and whatâs really at risk? As AI agents started reading, writing and acting on that data, they reached a conclusion that now looks obvious: securing AI means securing the data, the identities acting on it (human and non-human), and the agents themselves.

Put the two products side by side, and they complement each other perfectly. Cyera knows where the sensitive data is. Oasis knows who or what can actually touch it â every service account, API key and agent credential, and whether itâs behaving the way it should. Itâs a bit like a bank vault: the best way to protect it is by knowing both whatâs inside and whoâs approaching. Data security tells you whatâs actually at stake. Identity security tells you whether the thing touching your data is legitimate. Together, the two products cover the entire path an AI agent takes through a companyâs environment, from the data it touches to the identity it uses to touch it.

Thereâs a practical case here too. Cyera has built one of the most powerful enterprise GTM teams, with the kind of scale that usually takes a startup a decade to reach. Oasisâs product now gets to run through that engine, into enterprise accounts it would otherwise have taken years to earn on its own. And the market isnât waiting: Whoever builds the first genuinely complete AI security platform, spanning data, identity and agents, has a real shot at becoming the default layer enterprises standardize on as agentic AI rolls out. Speed and completeness both matter, and the combination of Cyera and Oasis creates both.

Sources indicate that the foundersâ backgrounds make the fit feel almost inevitable in hindsight. Itâs a small world: two teams weâd backed independently, drawn from the same pool of Israeli technical talent, ended up building the two halves of the same answer to AI security. Talpiot and Unit 8200 alumni have produced a disproportionate share of the last decadeâs big cybersecurity companies, so the coincidence is smaller than it looks, but itâs still a good sign when it plays out this cleanly.

In a recent development, danny, Amit and the Oasis team built the category-defining organization in non-human identity in under three years, from a standing start to a product enterprises trust with agentic access at scale. That doesnât happen without genuinely hard technical work, and a founder team that saw the shift to agentic AI before almost anyone else in security did. We at Sequoia have backed both Cyera and Oasis since their Series A rounds, and weâre proud to keep backing this team as they take on the next chapter together â a bigger stage, and an opportunity sized to match.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (919 w)

AI Solved Math’s Most Famous Problem. Now Humans Are Struggling to Understand It

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.
  • Recent findings suggest that levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude.
  • Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mathematicians are struggling to decode a 17-million-line solution to their field’s most famous problem, published by an Anthropic researcher on Friday.

Recent findings suggest that levent Alpöge released a proof in the programming language Lean of the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, which he had created with Claude. While the conjecture, which describes how prime numbers are distributed, is widely assumed to be true, many mathematicians have tried and failed to definitively show this, and the problem has become something of a holy grail of number theory.

Since Alpöge published his proof, more than 200 people have been collaborating to verify it. On Saturday, the nonprofit the Lean Focused Research Organization and volunteer-led organization Mathlib said on Saturday they have “full confidence” that the proof is sound. The problem is formulated correctly and the code compiles, they confirmed. Now, “we look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the newly introduced ideas in this proof,” they wrote.

In a recent development, lean proofs are written to be checked by machine, while mathematical papers are written to explain the results to the community so that they can be reviewed and advanced. But Alpöge hasn’t released the paper version, which clocks in at 250,000 pages and is, in his own estimation, a “travesty of slop.” (On Monday, he added in an X post that the Lean proof “is full of garbage obviously” but that it still “compiles.” He also remarked that the 250,000 pages was a “joke … I find big number [sic] extremely hilarious.”) That’s left mathematicians to their own devices as they try to decipher what newly introduced findings they can obtain and build from the result.

“Knowing there is a proof is one thing,” Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, tells WIRED, “but when we understand the proof, that would allow us to actually go beyond what has happened, to build upcoming branches of mathematics perhaps or formulate the next conjecture to push the horizon further.”.

In a recent development, saha reckons the community effort should be able to simplify the result into a human-readable form of under 10,000, if not 1,000, pages. But complicating this feat is the fact that the proof appears to draw on many advanced branches of number theory in a long and “incredibly counterintuitive” argument. “I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human,” claims Saha, “but AIs can do something completely different and almost alien, and that breaks our intuition about how very difficult mathematical results might come about.”.

Industry observers note that he was shocked to see even his own corner of number theory utilized by the proof, and has since been trying to understand how. Saha has been using OpenAI’s Astra model to convert sections of the Lean proof into more digestible formats, such as single-page posters like those presented at conferences and shorter documents. But there’s a limit to that approach.

“It may well be that no single person has the expertise to understand in detail every part of the proof,” he claims.

More than 60 other individuals are using AI agents to try to translate the Lean lines into understandable ideas on Principia Math, a collaborative platform designed to facilitate the understanding of AI breakthroughs. So far, they have done this for more than 3,000 pieces of the Lean proof, though platform chief executive officer Anton Shakov expects it will take mathematicians months before they have a good conceptual understanding of the proof Alpöge produced with Claude in roughly six weeks. “I personally believe the picture we will get in the end, once the ideas of this proof have been properly understood, will be astoundingly beautiful," he tells WIRED.

Independent mathematicians have already understood and written up one smaller result to have come out of Alpöge’s proof.

AI labs have previously been criticized for rushing to publish breakthrough mathematical results, claiming glory while leaving the academic community to digest the results—and clean up mistakes.

In a recent development, “No human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the Association for Human Mathematics, a group of more than 1,000 mathematicians founded in September, wrote in a statement on Friday of the 17-million-line opus. It complained that Alpöge’s announcement “builds upon over a century of human work, but fails to advance mathematical understanding in the same way.”.

Alpöge, who before joining Anthropic was a researcher at Harvard University, acknowledged on Friday what an “extraordinary” situation it was to present “the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighborhood around its mathematics,” and wrote that he would try his best to help digest the proof, including by writing it up properly. But having had to hold off from making the announcement ahead of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, “I just could not live if I waited even longer,” he wrote.

Anthropic rival OpenAI in October proved a weaker version of the problem, called the quasi-Riemann hypothesis. Alpöge had been scooped by OpenAI in September on another Millennium Prize Problem concerning the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe fluid motion. When the organization stated it had solved part of the problem, Alpöge’s collaborator, Fresh York University professor Tristan Buckmaster, claimed OpenAI had rushed ahead to beat the pair to it after becoming aware of his work. The pair also revealed on Friday that they had completed the remaining unsolved parts of the Navier-Stokes problem.

Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure.
  • But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
  • Industry observers note that in the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He stated he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

Industry observers note that in the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

“We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” claims Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

In a recent development, “This is a carbon copy of 2020,” said Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

The significant difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

On November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more vital than the voter! President DJT.”.

Industry observers note that election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and remarked the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also remarked he would speak directly to Trump about the challenges and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a new poll from UC San Diego.

Major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne stated over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

In a recent development, cybersecurity is a perpetual fight between the good guys and the bad. The age of agentic AI and Mythos-class models has tipped the scales in favor of the bad guys, opening a Pandoraâs box for offensive capabilities. An explosion in CVEs has since ensued.

According to recent reports, cyberattacks are about technical exploitation, which requires coding and reasoning prowess. Anthropicâs Mythos can discover and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Any model paired with a harness brings the cost of social engineering attacks down to near zero, unleashing them at unprecedented scale. The danger is heightened with every new model release.

Defensive security isnât improving in parallel. The relevant data lives in logs, events, traces and telemetry, a fundamentally different modality than the bodies of text LLMs usually train on, which barely show up in pretraining. Unlike offensive cybersecurity, which involves goal-directed reasoning towards a defined objective, defense requires open-ended reasoning, continually finding anomalies across vast amounts of normal-looking activity, a distinct capability that typically demands extensive domain-specific training. In short, defense is out of distribution for general-purpose frontier models: neither the data nor the intuition it requires is well-represented in training. In the race toward AGI, we cannot expect the frontier labs to take the detour of overhauling their training pipelines for defensive cybersecurity. And we certainly canât afford to bet our security on a hope that they do.

Industry observers note that corma has illustrated this âdefense gapâ in testing. They ran red/blue team simulations where an attacker plants a hidden backdoor and a defender tries to find it. The defender failed to find the backdoor 78% of the time, even when the defender was an identical copy of the very same model that planted it. Holding model quality constant, attackers will always have an advantage.

In a recent development, the only answer to scaling laws on offense is better scaling laws on defense. Recent events have shown that frontier AI for defensive cybersecurity is one of the crucial unsolved problems of the AI age. Solving it is the generational mission Corma was founded on.

Industry observers note that corma founder and CEO Alon Pluda and his team are training a foundation model to power defensive cybersecurity agents. Cybersecurity, like Go or chess, is a two-player, zero-sum game with a clean reward (were you breached or not?) and an endless supply of games to play. Reinforcement learning and self-play have produced superhuman results before in this kind of paradigm. We are seeing history repeat itself. Corma pushes this further with large-scale reinforcement learning across cybersecurity environments that replicate real enterprise networks, with all their tools, telemetry and noise â as part of a training pipeline that produces frontier defensive capabilities, outperforming general-purpose foundation models, with much lower per-token inference costs.

Industry observers note that in the cat-and-mouse game of cybersecurity, we believe Cormaâs vertical integration and âsovereign AIâ approach will win. Cost matters (always-on inference costs can rack up quickly). Owning the model weights matters (they arenât subject to restrictions on cybersecurity-related usage set by the closed model labs). And specialization and inference speed really matter (fastest to protect against a upcoming threat wins).

Cormaâs foundation model is deployed and productized as an agentic Security Workforce. These workers operate across different security tools and take on roles spanning the entire security organization: from security operations and identity management to cloud and network security and beyond. They are on the job at Fortune 500 companies and large enterprises across healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, retail and more.

Cormaâs foundation model powers agents that complete defensive work end to end. We spoke to one CISO whose Corma agent notified him of a pending attack through his Garmin watch while he was on a walk with his dog in the evening; with one confirmation, the agent was able to shut the attacker down, all while he was still walking. In another instance, within its first hour on the job, Corma uncovered, contained and remediated an active attacker campaign inside a customerâs network that their security team had missed for 52 days.

Industry observers note that training frontier foundation models for defensive cybersecurity requires world-class hackers and world-class researchers â almost no firm on earth has both. Alon is personally one of the most elite hackers in the world, and has assembled a cohesive and interdisciplinary team of hackers and researchers that is hill-climbing on technical challenges and building impressive commercial momentum.

We are thrilled to lead Cormaâs seed round and to be their partner as they chart upcoming territory in what is sure to be one of the most dynamic races in AI.

Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude.
  • In a recent development, the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold.
  • Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a upcoming mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” notes the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

In a recent development, the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she says.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a upcoming mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

The stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she says.

In a recent development, AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie says, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few concerns that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

It has been revealed that “It's the latest generational beef,” says Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in New York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

It has been revealed that lundquist states the matter has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

As a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

It has been revealed that her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she says. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

Others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He indicates his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

According to recent reports, “It can get heated,” notes John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

“Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” says Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those fresh to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll noted they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next massive step for every single person in the world.”.

According to recent reports, debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke states. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

Sources indicate that “He wants what's best for me,” Luke indicates. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

In the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

It has been revealed that when Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh says. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

Lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he states. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

In a recent development, his advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he states. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

If you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he claims. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

It has been revealed that intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he indicates. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made
